title: New duty takes effect to support children in temporary accommodation🏠

content.content: There are around 177,530 children living in temporary accommodation, the highest on record.

From today (1st September), a new duty takes effect, designed to enable these children to get the support they need as early as possible, and to stop vulnerable families from falling through the cracks.
WHAT'S THE PROBLEM? 📚
More families are living in temporary accommodation than ever before.
When a household is forced to move into temporary accommodation, it can be disruptive for children – affecting school attendance, healthcare appointments and access to support services.
Without the right join up between key services, support can come too late and children risk falling through the cracks.
The government wants to ensure that children experiencing homelessness receive the same opportunities and support as their peers, regardless of where they are living.
WHAT'S CHANGING? 🚀
From today, local authorities will be required to notify schools, GP practices and health visiting services when a child is placed in temporary accommodation.
To help councils implement the new duty quickly and effectively:
This means children staying engaged in education and ongoing connection to important health services – helping support wrap around families at the earliest stage.
HOW DOES THIS FIT INTO THE GOVERNMENT'S WIDER PLANS? 🏘️
The new duty is one part of the government's wider work to tackle homelessness and improve outcomes for vulnerable families.
It forms a key part of the National Plan to End Homelessness and sits alongside wider action to improve the experience of families living in temporary accommodation.
This includes £30 million of funding to reduce the use of B&Bs and improve the quality, suitability and long-term supply of temporary accommodation.

It also comes as the Prime Minister has launched a national drive to offer everyone sleeping rough a route off the streets this winter, backed by over £442 million to deliver more housing and specialist support.
It takes total investment in homelessness and rough sleeping services over the next three years to over £4 billion.
Reflecting on the news....
Homelessness Minister, Florence Eshalomi said:

“I know first-hand the uncertainty and upheaval that comes with not having a place to truly call home. For the thousands of children living in temporary accommodation, I know how much it can impact their school life, their ability to form lasting relationships and their sense of belonging.

“We’ve made clear that councils have a responsibility to place families in suitable, quality housing and from today, this will be matched with a new duty to inform education and health services when a child is homeless.

“This is a major milestone. Crucially, it means schools, GPs and councils all talking to each other about the vulnerable children in their community – ensuring vital support services are wrapped around them at the earliest opportunity and reducing the number of children falling through the cracks.”
Dr Laura Neilson, CEO of Shared Health Foundation said:

“I am delighted to see this notification be implemented. Education and health services want to support families living in temporary accommodation but have not known who the children are. That changes now.“I am grateful for colleagues in government and the civil service for their hard work and for the Minister championing this legislation. This is a key intervention to reduce the impact of homelessness on children, shine a light on them, and I believe it will save lives.”
Children’s Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza said:

“Every child deserves a safe, stable home and the opportunity to thrive, wherever they live. Children often fall through the gaps between services when they move between homes or move into temporary accommodation and face disruption to their education, healthcare and wider wellbeing.

“This new duty on local authorities is an important step towards making sure schools and health services know when a child moves into temporary accommodation, so they can put the right support in place. It is vital this duty is backed by a unique ID for every child, to help services join up information and ensure children do not lose access to the support they need whenever their circumstances change.”

title: Farmer Collaboration Fund: delivery partners can apply now

content.content: Delivery partners can now apply for the first round of the Farmer Collaboration Fund (FCF).
The £30 million fund will help farmers and land managers work together on local projects that improve productivity, sustainability and resilience.

Delivery partners are organisations with experience of supporting farmer collaboration. Funding will support them to establish new collaboration groups where there are gaps, support existing groups, appoint facilitators, share learning across the sector, and ensure funding is used effectively and transparently.
A summary of the fund
The FCF has been shaped through engagement with farmers, land managers and organisations across the sector.
At workshops held earlier this year, we heard that successful collaboration takes time and that groups need support to build relationships, develop shared priorities and turn ideas into action.

That's why successful delivery partners can receive funding for up to 3 years. This long-term approach reflects what we heard from farmers and gives groups the time and flexibility to develop projects that respond to local needs and opportunities.

For that reason, facilitators will provide direct support to farmer groups. They will co-ordinate meetings, arrange speakers and specialist advice, and help farmers agree shared actions. They may also support individual farmers where this contributes to the objectives of the wider group.

By working together, farmers can improve their businesses and deliver environmental benefits that would be difficult to achieve alone. This could include sharing machinery to reduce costs, adopting more efficient farming practices, and accessing funding opportunities such as Landscape Recovery.
Collaboration groups can also connect farmers with expert advice on issues including succession planning and business diversification.
To support collaboration and the sharing of ideas and experience, the FCF will fund activities including:
Applying
Guidance
Before beginning your application, read the Farmer Collaboration Fund applicant’s guide.
It explains:
Before applying, check that your organisation can meet the fund requirements and deliver the project for up to 3 years.
The guide explains the eligibility criteria for organisations, collaboration groups and activities, as well as the checks you will need to complete before submitting your application.
The application form
Once you've read the guidance, go to the Find a Grant page, and complete the application form using the portal. It's under the tab 'How to apply.'
The application form has 4 sections:
There is a form which contains templates for you to provide details of up to 20 supporting collaboration groups and a spreadsheet, where you can detail your spend.

You will also need to provide a milestone plan and roadmap in an attached file, as part of your application. This will help show what actions you will take to deliver the objectives you have identified.
Applicants who are unsuccessful in round 1 can apply again in round 2 if they meet the eligibility criteria.
If you need further help using the application portal, you can check the user guide, or contact the online helpdesk.
You can also call the helpdesk on 029 2279 0054. The phone line is open Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm, except public holidays.
Learn more
Webinar for applicants
To help you apply, we recently hosted a webinar for potential applicants.
The webinar explains the fund’s eligibility requirements, how to prepare a strong application and how applications will be assessed. It also includes answers to questions raised by attendees.
Watch the webinar
Webinar on the application portal
On Wednesday 9 September 2026, we're hosting another webinar designed to walk you through the application portal. There will be a live Q&A session where you can put your questions to the team.
Register to attend
It will start at 2:30pm and finish at 3:30pm.
Dates to note
We aim to share the successful projects by the end of the year. Subscribe to the Farming Blog, and you’ll receive a notification as soon as we publish this information.

description: Delivery partners can now apply for the Farmer Collaboration Fund. In this post, we share an overview, link to the guidance and details of webinars to learn more.

title: Capital Grants 2026 now closed

content.content: The Capital Grants 2026 offer is now closed as the budget has been allocated.

This year, £225 million was made available through Capital Grants 2026 to support practical environmental improvements on farms and across the countryside, representing a 50% increase on the 2025 budget.

We've received approximately 17,000 applications from every corner of England, covering a wide range of projects that will help deliver benefits for the environment, support nature recovery and strengthen sustainable farming practices.

The number of applications we received shows the appetite across the sector to invest in projects that will improve water quality, strengthen climate resilience, enhance biodiversity and protect the character of our rural landscapes.

We are now moving into the next stage of the process and have begun assessing applications and issuing agreements. Due to the high volume of applications received, it's likely that agreement offers will continue to be issued throughout the remainder of the year.
We will process applications as swiftly and efficiently as we can, but to help avoid delays, please ensure any requested supporting evidence and documentation is submitted as soon as possible.
All supporting information should be provided to the Rural Payments Agency (RPA) within 10 days of your application form being submitted.
As set out in the scheme guidance, any applications that were started but not submitted before the offer closed will not be processed.
If you have received a Capital Grant offer through this or a previous round but, due to a change in circumstances, no longer intend to carry out the work or claim the funding, please contact the RPA.
An early look at the data
The RPA monitors application data regularly. I wanted to share an early overview of what the early numbers indicate.
Figures have been rounded for clarity. As the scheme has only recently closed, application totals are still being finalised and may change slightly as remaining checks are completed.
Size of farms

From habitat creation and boundary restoration to water quality and resource management projects, applications reflected the important contribution farms of all sizes make to nature recovery and sustainable land management. One-third of applications have come from farms under 50 hectares (ha).
First-time applicants

One of the most encouraging figures we've seen is the number of first-time Capital Grant applicants this year. Of those who applied, approximately 9,500 were applying for a Capital Grants agreement for the first time. We're pleased to see so many new applicants engaging with the scheme, demonstrating growing awareness of the support available and the opportunities it offers to make practical improvements.
Popular items
Of the 80 items available in the offer, the most popular items were:

FG2 (Sheep Netting) is by far the most popular item, featuring in just over 11,000 submitted applications and accounting for approximately 20,000 km of fencing, roughly 1.5 times the Earth's diameter. The item is designed to protect sensitive habitats from grazing pressure, improve water quality by preventing livestock access to watercourses, and support the restoration and long-term management of priority habitats.

BN11 (Planting New Hedges) appears in approximately 5,000 applications, representing around 2,500 km of new hedgerows, roughly equivalent to the distance from Newcastle to Naples. These hedgerows will create vital wildlife corridors, providing food, shelter and nesting opportunities for birds, mammals and pollinators while helping to reconnect habitats across the landscape. Established with locally native species, they will create valuable new habitat, support biodiversity recovery and contribute to carbon capture, helping to protect, restore and enhance nature on farmland.

FG12 (Wooden Field Gate) featured in just over 4,500 applications. These gates support effective livestock management by controlling stock movement and preventing animals from entering sensitive areas where they could cause environmental damage. They also help protect important environmental, historic and archaeological features. In addition, wooden gate wings can provide secure, stock-proof crossing points over ditches, helping to maintain robust boundary management.

BN5 (Hedgerow Laying) appeared in around 2,500 applications, representing approximately 1,300 km of hedgerows, almost enough to stretch from Land's End to Hadrian’s Wall and back. The option restores mature hedges that have become gappy or overgrown, promoting healthy growth from the base to create dense, stock-proof boundaries. This helps reconnect hedgerow networks, providing valuable habitat and food sources for birds, bees and other pollinators, while supporting biodiversity recovery, carbon storage and the enhancement of nature across the farmed landscape.
Investing in the future
Although applications are still being processed, these figures provide an early indication of the ambition shown by farmers and land managers across England.

From restoring habitats and enhancing biodiversity to improving water quality and protecting historic features, the projects proposed have the potential to deliver lasting benefits for local communities, the natural environment and the long-term resilience of farm businesses.
As climate and weather-related pressures continue to grow, these practical improvements will help create a more sustainable and resilient countryside for future generations.
Next steps
While our immediate focus is on assessing applications and issuing agreements, we're also taking the opportunity to learn from this year's offer.
Working closely with colleagues in Defra, we're gathering feedback and reviewing customer experiences to understand where we can make improvements.

Whether it's feedback given when applicants call us, comments on our blog posts, or conversations with farmers and land managers at agricultural shows, we're listening carefully to what customers are telling us.

description: The 2026 Capital Grants offer is now closed. In this guest post, the Rural Payments Agency's Chief Executive, Oliver Munn, shares some early reflections on the data and the environmental ambition they represent.

title: Supporting devolution through digital, data and AI
authors: Emily Middleton, Director General for Digital Transformation

content.content: Across government, there is a growing focus on how powers, funding and decision-making can be exercised closer to the places they impact. As this evolves, one thing is becoming increasingly clear: digital, data and AI will play an important role in helping local leaders deliver services effectively and achieve better outcomes for their communities.

At the Government Digital Service (GDS), we're pleased to be working with Mayoral Strategic Authorities, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) and No.10 North through a new Digital Devolution programme, announced on 21 August by the Prime Minister. The programme is designed to support places with some of the key digital and data foundations and the products and services needed to deliver their priorities, whilst helping central and local government work together more effectively.
Digital is increasingly part of the delivery challenge

Over recent months we've been speaking with digital and data leaders from Strategic Authorities across England. While every place is different, a number of common themes have emerged. Data sharing remains a significant challenge. Too often organisations working with the same residents cannot easily share information, making it harder to deliver joined-up services and target support effectively.

Many authorities are managing varied technology estates and levels of digital maturity. There is strong interest in the potential of AI, but also a recognition that capability, governance and workforce skills need to develop alongside technology adoption.

We've also seen some excellent examples of innovation already underway locally. Authorities are developing regional data platforms, investing in digital capability, experimenting with AI and creating new partnerships across public services. A consistent message from those conversations has been that local leaders want practical support, stronger collaboration and a clear route for working with central government on shared challenges.
Turning discussion into practical action

Over the next three months, we'll work with Strategic Authorities on a set of activities focused on exploring unlocking access to data and strengthening digital capability. These activities build on existing work already under way across government and local government, and aim to address some of the barriers that authorities have identified themselves.

This includes working with Strategic Authorities in support of the recommendations from the Milburn Review to support young people into training and jobs, on blocked data journeys - helping identify and resolve barriers that can make data difficult to access or use. We'll do this by bringing together digital and data leaders across government and Strategic Authorities, through data access workshops and data readiness diagnostics with localities, and work towards reusable data sharing agreement models that can help simplify engagement between central government and Strategic Authorities.

Support also includes holding events such an Early Years Digital and Data Innovation Day in Sheffield on 9 September together with South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority, bringing together local and national partners to explore how digital and data can support improved outcomes for children and families, and continuing work with departments and Strategic Authorities to support young people into employment, training and education.

Alongside this, we'll invest in capability through initiatives such as local government AI and Data Science Skills Accelerators, AI Engineers in Residence, Get Tech Certified and a new AI Places Accelerator. These programmes are designed to help Strategic Authorities develop the skills, confidence and capacity needed to use digital, data and AI effectively in delivering local priorities. We will also work with partners to strengthen cyber security and data governance capability across Strategic Authorities.
Building the longer-term foundations

One of the strongest messages from our engagement with Strategic Authorities has been the importance of working together on the longer-term conditions that will support public service delivery across organisational boundaries. Common standards, interoperable data, re-usable products, architectural vision, strong cyber security, digital capability and shared approaches to solving common problems all have an important role to play.

Addressing these challenges will require coordinated action across local and national government. GDS is well placed to support that effort, bringing together expertise, sharing learning from what works, and helping to address common barriers that no single organisation can tackle alone. By strengthening the digital and data foundations that underpin public service delivery, we can help Strategic Authorities move faster, make better use of technology and focus on what matters most to them: delivering better outcomes for the communities they serve.

That's why the Digital Devolution programme is not simply a set of individual initiatives. It is an opportunity to bring together local and national leaders to shape a longer-term digital and data agenda. In doing so we’ll draw together a two-year digital and data devolution strategy and roadmap as part of the forthcoming Devolution White paper.

We're looking forward to working more closely with Strategic Authorities and local government as this programme develops, and to continuing the conversation about how digital, data and AI can support better public services across the country.

title: From sustainability champions to sustainability by design – Part One

content.content: Sustainable ICT is becoming central to how we design, buy, run and improve digital services. The question now is how we turn good intentions into everyday practice — moving from sustainability being driven by individual champions to making it part of how decisions are made from the very start.
Over the last decade, sustainability has become an increasingly important part of conversations about digital services, technology and ICT across government and industry.

Since around 2015, I have seen growing awareness of sustainable ICT practices, driven largely by passionate individuals, local initiatives, and examples of good practice. These efforts have achieved a great deal. They have helped raise awareness, demonstrate what is possible and encourage organisations to think differently about the environmental impact of digital services.
However, they have also highlighted a challenge.

Too often, progress has relied on individual champions rather than being embedded into the systems and processes that shape everyday decision-making. As a result, organisations can develop different approaches, varying levels of maturity and multiple ways of measuring success.

If sustainability is to become truly business as usual, I believe we need to move beyond treating it as a separate activity and instead make it an integral part of how we design, acquire, deliver, and operate digital services.
One principle that has shaped my thinking over the years is - sustainability by design, not sustainability by exception

If sustainability requires a separate process, additional approvals, or specialist intervention every time a decision is made, it risks becoming something that is considered only when time and resources allow.
My experience suggests that the most effective approach is to build sustainability into the processes that already exist.

Rather than creating parallel structures, sustainability should be considered within governance, investment decisions, requirements management, architecture reviews, commercial activity, programme delivery, assurance processes, and service management.
The aim should be simple: make the sustainable choice the easiest and most natural choice.
Moving beyond additional processes
One of the lessons I have learned is that creating more sustainability processes does not always lead to better sustainability outcomes.

Over the years, organisations have introduced a variety of frameworks, maturity assessments, and reporting tools. Many have been developed with the best intentions, and some have delivered real value. However, they can struggle to gain traction when they operate alongside existing delivery and governance arrangements rather than within them.
In practice, this can create additional reporting requirements without necessarily improving decision-making.

A more effective approach is often to integrate sustainability into activities that organisations already undertake. Business case approvals, architecture reviews, portfolio reporting, supplier management, assurance activities, and service management processes all provide opportunities to consider sustainability without creating additional layers of administration.
When sustainability becomes part of normal business activity rather than an additional task, it is far more likely to influence decisions and become embedded over the long term.
Making better use of information we already have
Good decisions rely on good information, and consistent approaches to sustainability reporting remain important.
At the same time, I believe we should be cautious about creating unnecessary new reporting burdens.

Many suppliers already provide sustainability-related information through contract delivery, performance reporting, and corporate disclosures. Rather than requesting the same information through separate channels, there is often an opportunity to make better use of what is already available.

For example, sustainability data can be discussed during routine supplier performance meetings, service reviews and governance forums, alongside more traditional measures such as cost, performance, and delivery outcomes.
This helps reduce duplication while increasing the likelihood that sustainability information is actively considered when decisions are made.
In Part Two Christopher will be explaining the benefits of thinking about sustainability earlier, and the opportunities this presents.
More information
Christopher Gale is an Acquisition Safety and Environmental Manager, Digital & Data, at the Ministry of Defence.
If you're interested in finding out more about what we do check out our LinkedIn page for all the latest news, stories and job openings. While you're there, why not give us a follow?
Like what you read? Subscribe to the blog for all the latest updates.

title: Small R&D Partnerships competition now open

content.content: The Small Research and Development Partnerships competition is now open, with £13 million available to support collaborative projects.
This is round 5 of the competition, delivered through the Farming Innovation Programme in partnership with Innovate UK.
It forms part of the government’s Industrial Strategy commitment to allocate at least £200 million to the programme up to 2030.

The competition gives research organisations and businesses the opportunity to work alongside farmers, growers and foresters to develop new farming products or services, bringing them closer to commercial use.
Projects must benefit England’s agricultural, horticultural or forestry sectors by improving productivity, environmental sustainability and resilience.
Overview

Small R&D Partnerships support collaborative projects that show an idea already works in practice. The funding can help project teams develop their product or service further and bring it closer to market.
We have not set specific topics or themes for projects. Instead, we want to support solutions that respond to the priorities identified by the industry.
A UK-registered business must lead the project. It can last up to 30 months and must have total eligible costs of between £1 million and £3 million.
Projects should develop practical solutions that can:
The project team must include at least one other business or research organisation, and farmers, growers or foresters must be involved throughout.
How to apply
Before applying, read the competition guidance on the Innovation Funding Service to check the full eligibility, scope and funding rules.
You can also learn more about R&D Partnerships through the Farming Innovation Programme, including how to build a project team and involve farmers, growers or foresters.
To help you prepare your application, Innovate UK recently recorded an applicant webinar to learn about the aims, scope and content of the competition. Watch the recording.
The window to apply closes 14 October 2026.
Case studies
The following projects showcase a range of work supported through previous Small R&D Partnerships rounds.
Developing a vaccine to protect pigs from Streptococcus suis
Disease remains a significant challenge for pig producers, affecting animal welfare, productivity and farm costs.
Streptococcus suis can cause serious and sometimes fatal disease in pigs and people. Outbreaks can increase antibiotic use and contribute to antimicrobial resistance.
Led by The Vaccine Group (TVG), this small R&D funded project developed a vaccine to protect pigs against multiple strains, or serotypes, of Streptococcus suis.
It used a harmless virus to deliver a protein shared by different serotypes, prompting an immune response without exposing pigs to the disease-causing bacterium.

The vaccine showed protection against serotype 2, the strain responsible for most Streptococcus suis in UK pigs, as well as immune responses to other serotypes. The project tested whether the vaccine could also protect against serotype 1, including through studies involving commercial pig breeds.
The Vaccine Group reported that a trial conducted at Moredun Scientific Ltd has already shown great results, with the vaccine outperforming a leading commercially available vaccine.
Using hoverflies to control aphids in soft fruit

Berry growers face increasing pressure from aphids and other pests, while fewer conventional chemical controls are available. Aphids can be particularly difficult to manage in crops grown under tunnels, glass or other protected environments, where dense foliage can make infestations harder to reach.

Led by Pollinator and Orchard Management, also known as Olombria, FLYTHRIVE is developing a new approach to pest management using native hoverflies. Adult hoverflies can move through dense crops and lay eggs near aphid colonies. Their larvae then feed on the aphids, with a single larva able to consume hundreds during its development.

The project is testing blends of native hoverfly species against aphids that damage protected soft fruit crops. It combines this biological control with vision machines that can detect pests, monitor predators and natural attractants. This means that hoverflies can be directed towards infestations at an early stage.

The project brings together commercial growers, applied researchers and agritech specialists, including Niab, the Natural Resources Institute at the University of Greenwich, Asplins Producer Organisation and The Summer Berry Company. Field and controlled-environment trials are helping the team test and refine the system in commercial growing conditions.

By strengthening natural pest control and supporting earlier, more targeted intervention, FLYTHRIVE aims to help growers protect yields, reduce labour and chemical inputs, and produce fruit more sustainably. The approach could also have applications in other fruit crops and protected growing systems.
Developing bio-derived fungicides to protect wheat from septoria

Septoria, caused by the fungal pathogen Zymoseptoria tritici, is one of the most damaging diseases affecting UK winter wheat. It can significantly reduce yields if left unmanaged. As resistance to some existing fungicides increases, growers need new ways to protect crops and maintain productivity.

Led by Bactobio, the project is developing bio-derived fungicides using compounds produced by microbes. Its technology combines next-generation sequencing, machine learning and bioengineering to culture microbial species that have historically been difficult to grow and study in laboratory conditions.

Researchers are expanding the company’s microbial library and building a system to identify compounds that could control Zymoseptoria tritici. The most promising microbes are being profiled, tested and scaled up to support further development.

The project aims to produce 3 to 5 potential fungicides. The team will then test them in small-plot field trials. This will help identify the strongest candidates for further testing, commercial development and eventual on-farm use.
By creating new bio-derived fungicides, the project aims to help wheat growers protect yields, manage fungicide resistance and reduce the environmental impact of crop protection.

title: Help shape the future of food safety: Join an FSA Scientific Advisory Committee
authors: Professor Ian Young CBE, Chief Scientific Adviser

content.content: Cymraeg

In my role as Chief Scientific Adviser at the Food Standards Agency (FSA), I would like to invite you to help shape the future of food safety by joining one of the FSA's Scientific Advisory Committees.

At the FSA we are committed to ensuring that food is safe, authentic, healthier and more sustainable. Science sits at the heart of everything we do, helping us make evidence-based decisions that protect consumers and support a trusted food system.
This is why I am delighted to encourage you to apply for membership of one of our Scientific Advisory Committees, including the Science Council.
What is the role of the FSA’s Scientific Advisory Committees?
Our committees provide independent scientific advice on a wide range of issues, from food and feed safety to microbiological risks, toxicity of chemicals, novel foods, and emerging technologies.
Their expertise helps ensure that FSA policies and decisions are informed by the best available evidence and reflect the latest scientific developments.
Who are we looking for?

We are seeking individuals with a broad range of scientific knowledge, skills, and experience including pathology, neurotoxicity, microbiology, proteomic and metabolomic analysis, animal feed safety, chemical contaminants in food, social science and more.

Whether you are at the beginning of your career, an established expert in your field, or have specialist expertise that can bring a fresh perspective to our discussions, we encourage you to consider applying.
We are particularly keen to attract applicants from diverse professional backgrounds, sectors, and communities to ensure our committees benefit from a wide range of viewpoints and experiences.
Why should you consider applying?
Serving on an FSA Scientific Advisory Committee is a unique opportunity to contribute to issues of national importance, work alongside leading experts, and help shape the future of UK food policies.
It is also a rewarding way to apply your expertise in the public interest and make a tangible difference to consumers.
Additionally, if you’re a university employee, this role can contribute to your next Research Excellence Framework (REF) return.
When/how can you apply?
We are actively recruiting throughout September and until 12 October 2026.
Details of the vacancies and more information on how you can apply can be found on GOV.UK.

Please also help us spread the word by sharing these vacancies with colleagues and professional networks. Together, we can continue to ensure that the UK's food system is underpinned by world-class scientific advice.

Yn rhinwedd fy swydd fel Prif Gynghorydd Gwyddonol yr Asiantaeth Safonau Bwyd (ASB), hoffwn eich gwahodd i helpu i lunio dyfodol diogelwch bwyd drwy ymuno ag un o Bwyllgorau Cynghori Gwyddonol yr ASB.

Yn yr ASB rydyn ni wedi ymrwymo i sicrhau bod bwyd yn ddiogel, yn ddilys, yn iachach ac yn fwy cynaliadwy. Mae gwyddoniaeth wrth wraidd popeth a wnawn, gan ein helpu i wneud penderfyniadau ar sail tystiolaeth er mwyn diogelu defnyddwyr a chefnogi system fwyd y gellir ymddiried ynddi.
Dyna pam rwy’n falch iawn o’ch annog i wneud cais i fod yn aelod o un o’n Pwyllgorau Cynghori Gwyddonol, gan gynnwys y Cyngor Gwyddoniaeth.
Beth yw rôl Pwyllgorau Cynghori Gwyddonol yr ASB?

Mae ein pwyllgorau yn darparu cyngor gwyddonol annibynnol ar ystod eang o faterion, o ddiogelwch bwyd a bwyd anifeiliaid i risgiau microbiolegol, gwenwyndra cemegion, bwydydd newydd, a thechnolegau sy’n dod i’r amlwg.
Mae eu harbenigedd yn helpu i sicrhau bod polisïau a phenderfyniadau’r ASB yn cael eu llywio gan y dystiolaeth orau sydd ar gael ac yn adlewyrchu’r datblygiadau gwyddonol diweddaraf.
Am bwy rydyn ni’n chwilio?

Rydyn ni’n chwilio am unigolion sydd ag ystod eang o wybodaeth, sgiliau a phrofiad gwyddonol, gan gynnwys ym meysydd patholeg, niwrowenwyndra, microbioleg, dadansoddi proteomig a metabolomig, diogelwch bwyd anifeiliaid, halogion cemegol mewn bwyd, gwyddor gymdeithasol a mwy.

P’un a ydych chi ar ddechrau’ch gyrfa, yn arbenigwr sefydledig yn eich maes, neu fod gennych chi arbenigedd a all ddod â safbwynt newydd i’n trafodaethau, rydyn ni’n eich annog i ystyried gwneud cais.
Rydyn ni’n arbennig o awyddus i ddenu ymgeiswyr o gymunedau, sectorau a chefndiroedd proffesiynol amrywiol, er mwyn sicrhau bod ein pwyllgorau’n elwa o ystod eang o safbwyntiau a phrofiadau.
Pam dylech chi ystyried gwneud cais?

Mae gwasanaethu ar un o Bwyllgorau Cynghori Gwyddonol yr ASB yn gyfle unigryw i gyfrannu at faterion sydd o bwys cenedlaethol, i weithio ochr yn ochr ag arbenigwyr blaenllaw, ac i helpu i lunio dyfodol polisïau bwyd y DU.
Mae hefyd yn ffordd werth chweil o roi’ch arbenigedd ar waith er budd y cyhoedd ac o wneud gwahaniaeth gwirioneddol i ddefnyddwyr.
Yn ogystal, os ydych chi’n gweithio mewn prifysgol, gall y rôl hon gyfrannu at eich ffurflen nesaf ar gyfer y Fframwaith Rhagoriaeth Ymchwil (REF).
Pryd/Sut gallwch chi wneud cais?
Byddwn ni wrthi’n recriwtio drwy gydol mis Medi hyd nes 12 Hydref 2026.
Mae manylion y swyddi gwag a mwy o wybodaeth am sut gallwch chi wneud cais ar gael ar GOV.UK.

Hefyd, a fyddech cystal â’n helpu ni i ledaenu’r gair drwy rannu’r swyddi gwag hyn gyda chydweithwyr a rhwydweithiau proffesiynol? Gyda’n gilydd, gallwn ni barhau i sicrhau bod system fwyd y DU yn cael ei hategu gan gyngor gwyddonol o’r radd flaenaf.

title: Back to school with IP

content.content: School’s starting soon, it’s a big part of your every year beginning. Whether you're heading to secondary school, college or university, it's a time for new experiences, new trends and, of course, new school supplies.

We're Arwen and Freya, and we're spending our work experience with the Intellectual Property Office (IPO) social media team. Today, we're taking over the IPO Blog to share what we've learned about intellectual property (IP) and uncover the protection behind the everyday items we use at school. What do pens, pencils, notebooks and backpacks have in common? They can all be protected by IP.
Get ready for school with us

One of the first things we make sure we get right for the new school year is our shoes. We need something comfortable enough to wear all day, whether we're in lessons, walking between classes or spending time with friends.

This year we both chose to go with Nike trainers. Nike uses trade marks to protect its brand, including protecting their name and iconic 'Swoosh' logo. Nike trade marks help customers recognise Nike products and identify the business they come from.
Next up is bags
Although we're both getting ready for the new school year, our choices for bags are very different. Freya's going for a Coach bag, while Arwen's go-to bag is a Vans backpack.

Coach is a well known luxury brand. While the sizes can be big or small, totes are the way to go during these times. It’s big and practical – perfect for carrying all of your back to school equipment. Coach has protected its logo and name with a trademark. Check out some of their trade marks: Coach’s Trade marks

Vans has built a strong and recognisable brand, protecting its identity through a portfolio of trade marks including its famous logo. These trade marks help customers identify genuine Vans products and distinguish them from other brands.

Trade marks can protect names, logos and slogans. They help businesses protect their brands and help customers recognise where products and services come from. Find out more about trade marks and how to apply: Register a trade mark : Overview - GOV.UK
Inside our pencil case

One of the most important things for life in education is your stationery. Our go-to stationery is Staedtler. The brand is known for its Norris pencils which are famously known as the black and yellow ones that many people across the UK will recognise from their classrooms and pencil cases.
The Noris name is protected by a trade mark, helping Staedtler protect its brand and making it easier for customers to identify genuine products.

Staedtler has also used registered designs to protect the appearance of some of its products. Design protection can cover the look of an item, helping businesses safeguard features that make their products distinctive.
The smart board that powers our lessons

One piece of technology that has become a common sight in classrooms is the smart board. These interactive displays allow teachers and students to write, draw and interact with digital content directly on the screen, helping to make lessons more engaging.
Technology like this is often protected by patents. A patent protects new inventions and gives the owner the right to stop others from making, using or selling the invention without permission

Our work experience at the IPO has shown us that intellectual property is everywhere — even in the classroom. Trade marks, designs and patents all play a part in protecting the products we rely on, helping businesses stay innovative and helping consumers trust what they buy. As we head into the new school year, we will think about the items in our bags that have more behind them than meets the eye.

description: School's starting soon! Work experience students Arwen and Freya are taking over the IPO blog to explore the intellectual property behind their back-to-school essentials.

title: One week left to apply for roles on UK National Screening Committee

content.content: There is just one week left for people to apply for one of 4 vacancies on the UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC).
The UK NSC is looking to appoint 4 new expert members to support its work advising ministers and the NHS in the 4 UK countries about all aspects of screening.
The independent scientific committee is looking for individuals with a track record of national achievements in one of the following 4 roles:
How to apply
To find out more, including how to apply, please see the role descriptions and candidate information pack.
The closing date for applications is midday on Tuesday 8 September 2026.
Completed applications should be emailed to appointments.team@dhsc.gov.uk.
For any enquiries, please email  uknsc@dhsc.gov.uk
UK NSC and its host organisation the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) value and promote diversity. We encourage applications from all sections of the community.
About the roles

As well as specialist skills in their own particular area, candidates should be able to understand and critically consider complex information and scientific and/or medical data and have excellent communication skills.
Lay members should have the desire to make an effective contribution as a representative of all patients, carers and members of the public. See additional information about the role of PPV members.
Post holders are not paid but do receive travel and other related expenses.
Appointment term: successful candidates are usually appointed for a 3-year term, up to a maximum of 3 terms (totalling 9 years).

Commitment: The UK NSC meets 3 times a year to discuss and agree screening recommendations. Members are also required to engage in the development of documents relating to committee business throughout their term.
Keep up to date

The UK NSC blog provides up to date news from the UK NSC. You can register to receive updates direct to your inbox, so there is no need to keep checking for new articles. If you have any questions about this blog article, or about the work of the UK NSC, please email uknsc@dhsc.gov.uk.
